AI and .NET

.NET developers across the globe — from London to Lagos, India to Italy— face a shared set of issues. Performance can make or break an app; it might run smoothly under light use, but crank up the load, and can issue emerge. Scalability is just as critical — designing for growth is one thing, but keeping things stable during a traffic is a different beast. Then there’s the demand for advanced capabilities: businesses want apps that don’t just process data but predict outcomes, like forecasting inventory needs, without you manually coding every rule. These are universal pain points, whether you’re a freelancer or part of a multinational team.

Artificial intelligence steps up as a practical solution. AI can boost performance by handling intensive computations, simplify scaling with dynamic resource allocation, and deliver predictive power — like anticipating demand or optimizing workflows — all without requiring you to be an AI expert. For .NET developers everywhere, two tools stand out:

Azure OpenAI Service and ML.NET.

Azure OpenAI Service

is Microsoft’s cloud platform, giving you access to OpenAI’s advanced models — the same tech behind ChatGPT — via simple API calls. Hosted on Azure’s global network, it’s a ready-to-use service for tasks like generating insights or processing complex data.

ML.NET

is a free, open-source .NET library for custom machine learning. It lets you build models to predict trends or classify data, all in C#, enhancing your existing skills. These tools are built for .NET devs worldwide, making AI a reality from São Paulo to Sydney.

✨The Integration: .NET and AI in Practice

What ties .NET and AI together so well? .NET 9, launched in November 2024, brings serious performance — building on .NET 8’s 30% faster AI inference — and Azure’s cloud scales it effortlessly across 60+ regions. A cohesive stack that works wherever you’re coding, whether on Windows, macOS, or Linux.

Let’s try creating a Predictive Inventory Forecasting. Imagine you’re building a .NET 9 app for a retail chain — could be in Berlin, Bangalore, or Buenos Aires. The goal is to predict how much stock each store needs next month, avoiding overstock or shortages. With Azure OpenAI Service, you can tap into its reasoning models (like the o1 series for now ) to analyze sales data and trends. Here’s how it unfolds, laid out clearly.

Your app collects historical sales data — say, “Store A sold 500 units of Product X in January, 600 in February” — plus external factors like holidays or weather. You want Azure OpenAI to crunch this and forecast March demand. The model doesn’t just guess; it reasons through patterns, something traditional code struggles to replicate without heavy lifting.

The process:

  • Data Prep: Your app gathers sales figures and context (e.g., “Easter’s in March this year”).
  • Request: It sends a structured prompt to Azure OpenAI — think “Given sales of 500 in Jan, 600 in Feb, and Easter in March, predict Product X demand.” — via an HTTP call.
  • Analysis: The o1 model processes it, factoring in trends and events, and returns a number, like “750 units.”
  • Action: Your app uses that to adjust orders or alert managers, all in real time.

Why does this work?

.NET 9’s speed keeps the app responsive, even with big datasets. Azure’s global reach and scalability mean it handles multiple stores or regions without flinching. You’re coding in C#, using familiar tools, and deploying to Azure with ease. ML.NET could build a custom model if you had unique data, but Azure OpenAI’s reasoning power delivers fast, smart results out of the box.

Why This Matters Globally

— For All Devs, With Code to Start

What’s the payoff for you, no matter where you’re based? Whether you’re new to .NET or an expert, AI with .NET opens doors. Let’s break it down and cap it with a working code example you can run yourself.

🔹For newcomers —

this is an accessible entry point. Azure OpenAI’s API-first design means you’re not decoding AI algorithms; you’re just calling a service, like any REST endpoint. .NET 9’s lightweight features, like minimal APIs, let you build fast without getting bogged down. ML.NET’s Visual Studio tools even offer a no-code way to dip into machine learning. You’re solving real problems early, building skills that travel anywhere.

🔹For experienced devs —

this is about scale and impact. You’re likely managing complex systems: supply chains, financial platforms, or IoT networks. Azure’s reliability (99.9% uptime) and .NET 9’s performance let you deploy AI-powered apps globally. Security’s covered with private networking, and Azure’s pricing updates keep costs manageable. Your .NET expertise plugs right in, turning big challenges into efficient solutions.

Here’s a .NET 9 console app that calls Azure OpenAI to forecast demand. It’s simple, functional, and yours to try:

using System;
using System.Net.Http;
using System.Text;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

class Program
{
    static async Task Main()
    {
        // Your Azure OpenAI endpoint and key from the portal
        string endpoint = "https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/<your-deployment>/chat/completions?api-version=2024-09-01-preview";
        string apiKey = "<your-api-key>";
        string prompt = "Given sales of 500 units in Jan, 600 in Feb, and Easter in March, predict demand for Product X in March.";

        // HTTP client setup
        using var client = new HttpClient();
        client.DefaultRequestHeaders.Add("api-key", apiKey);

        // Request payload
        var payload = new
        {
            messages = new[]
            {
                new { role = "user", content = prompt }
            },
            max_completion_tokens = 20
        };

        string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(payload);
        var content = new StringContent(json, Encoding.UTF8, "application/json");

        // Send and process response
        HttpResponseMessage response = await client.PostAsync(endpoint, content);
        if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
        {
            string result = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
            var jsonResult = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<JsonElement>(result);
            string forecast = jsonResult.GetProperty("choices")[0]
                .GetProperty("message")
                .GetProperty("content")
                .GetString();
            Console.WriteLine($"Forecasted Demand: {forecast.Trim()}");
        }
        else
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Error: {response.StatusCode} - {await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync()}");
        }
    }
}
Next time we will simplify it more so that your code will look more cleaner using Azure AI Library

How It Works:

  1. Setup: Create an Azure OpenAI resource, deploy a model (e.g., o1 or GPT-4o), and grab your endpoint and key.
  2. Project: Use dotnet new console for a .NET 9 app. Standard libraries are included.
  3. Config: Replace endpoint and apiKey
  4. Run: In Visual Studio, hit F5, or use dotnet run. Expect something like “Forecasted Demand: 750 units.”
  5. Debug:

401? Check your key.

429? You’ve hit rate limits — wait or adjust your Azure plan.

This is your starting point— beginners can play with the prompt, pros can scale it into a service. AI and .NET empower you to predict, optimize, and deliver, wherever your code takes you.
